issues.issue: "The present contract" is not identified by date or title, and the only contract booklet elsewhere referenced is the expired 1981-84 booklet (paragraph 14), so what body of terms the six-year "Contract" consists of is left open. The reader cannot tell from these words whether side letters and memoranda are part of the "present contract" or only preserved separately by paragraph 14.

The "additional $3.67 per shift from wages and after taxes ... shall be contributed to the Welfare Fund" does not say whose money it is — an employer contribution or an employee wage deduction remitted to the Fund — nor whether it is owed for shifts beyond the five-shift maximum. That characterization determines the size of the employer's contribution obligation.

The same $3.67 is described in the Section 13-H.1 amendment (Appendix, "add 'and an after tax deduction from wages of $3.67'") as a deduction from wages rather than as a contribution to the Welfare Fund, and the two descriptions cannot both be given literal effect. A court asked how much is owed to the Fund would have to reconcile paragraph 2(a) with that amendment.

Paragraph 2(a) expressly directs that "Pension and welfare contributions shall be made on this amount" for the 1987 increase, while paragraph 2(b) states the 1989-1992 increases with no such direction, inviting a negative-implication argument that contributions are not owed on them. The relationship between the two subparagraphs, not the figures, is what would be construed.

The clause fixes no formula, base period or multiplier for the cost-of-living adjustment, deferring wholly to unspecified "relevant provisions of the Contract," and the bracketed Index sentence does not say whether the measurement runs May-to-May or January-to-January. The 1992 Memorandum's later stipulation that adjustments "utilize a January to January rather than a May to May Index" shows the gap.

The opening sentence is incomplete — "shall have full force and effect at the Edison, New Jersey [gap] by The Times within the Northeast Corridor" — so the class of facilities covered (Edison only, or every new or rebuilt plant in the Corridor) cannot be read off the words. The later garbled passage about listing protected regular situation holders leaves the same scope question open.

"Any issues under this paragraph" has no fixed referent: the mediation sentence sits in a separate block from numbered paragraph 3, so it is unclear whether mediation reaches only new/rebuilt-facility arbitrations or all disputes under paragraph 3. The command that "the arbitrator shall issue his award before operations commence" is also stated as mandatory yet immediately assumes he may not.

The me-too right is keyed to "any labor organization" followed by a parenthetical list of nine named unions, leaving it open whether the list is exhaustive (expressio unius) or merely illustrative. "Wage and benefit package" is likewise undefined as against the productivity/attrition and diversion provisos.

The obligation is to execute such documents "as are necessary to administer" the Welfare Fund, an open-ended standard with an illustrative "including but not limited to" list, so what The Times must actually sign is undetermined. Whether that reaches the Fund's trust agreement and its delinquency machinery is left to argument.

As with 5(a), the duty to execute documents "as are necessary to administer" the Pension Fund states no standard for necessity and no limit on the documents covered. The Fund's own trust agreement (Article 9) purports to govern rate, mode and enforcement of contributions, so what 5(b) commits The Times to is uncertain.

The disclaimer that nothing requires The Times "to expend any funds beyond its obligation to make contributions" is hard to square with the Fund trust agreement's Article 9.4, which imposes interest, liquidated damages and collection costs on a delinquent employer. A delinquency defendant would invoke 5(c) as capping its exposure at contributions alone.

"Various shop disputes" is not identified, and the provision's whole content depends on Appendix A, whose heading in the executed document is garbled. Which disputes were resolved, and whether anything outside Appendix A survives, cannot be told from the text.

The nondiscrimination ground list — color, race, sex, religion, national origin — is closed, with no catch-all, so age, disability and other protected characteristics are excluded by negative implication. "Any other condition of employment" is also undefined against the specific reference to hiring.

The paragraph recites that Section 3-H.2 coverage is being raised "from $60,000," but Section 3-H.2 of the 1981-84 Collective Bargaining Agreement states $20,000, and $50,000 beginning January 1, 1982. The premise of the increase cannot be squared with the section it amends, leaving the covered class and prior amount in doubt.

"Group I employees not so scheduled" has no antecedent anywhere in this Memorandum — the scheduling premise lives only in Section 13-J of the Collective Bargaining Agreement — so the class covered by the new jury-pay formula is unstated. It is also unclear whether the eight-week look-back replaces or supplements the existing differential pay.

"Plants" is capitalized but undefined, and the revision changes Section 6-D from "more than one plant" to "one or more Plants," so whether a staging facility, annex or the 43rd Street building counts as a plant is open. The disjunctive "foreman or assistant foreman" also leaves the required rank indeterminate.

The letter is said to be "attached as Appendix C," but the executed document labels its attachments only "Appendix A" and "Appendix B," and the weekly-contribution letter carries no Appendix C designation. Which writing paragraph 11 incorporates has to be worked out from the instrument as a whole.

The Section 3-P letter is said to be "attached as Appendix D," yet no attachment in the executed document bears that label, the 3-P letter appearing between two blocks marked "Appendix B." The cross-reference cannot be matched to the papers actually annexed.

Paragraph 13 refers to a letter of understanding "attached as Appendix E," but the only arbitrator-related letter in the document (the neutrals-designation letter) is marked Appendix B and fixes no designations. What the parties agreed to execute cannot be identified from the attachments.

Paragraph 14 preserves "all letter agreements, side agreements ... in effect on the date hereof," which cannot be squared with Appendix A's abolition of the November 22, 1983 West Side Direct Routes Memorandum and with the September 9, 1988 letter saying that abolition leaves the rest of that memorandum intact. Which instrument controls the West Side Direct routes turns on reading the three together.

Paragraph 15 contemplates a later-executed "New York Times Agreement" embodying the modified Contract, while paragraph 1 says the Contract simply is the present contract as changed by this Memorandum; if the new document was never executed or departs from the Memorandum, the two provisions point to different governing texts. Paragraph 14's supremacy sentence does not say which prevails over a subsequently executed consolidated document.

Effectiveness "immediately following Union ratification" is hard to square with paragraph 1's term running from March 31, 1987 and paragraph 2's increases and Welfare Fund contributions made "effective March 31, 1987" in a document signed in August 1988. Which obligations run from ratification and which retroactively is left to construction.

The chapeau condition — "subject to there being no increase in the number of floor hires as set forth in the Collective Bargaining Agreement" — sits awkwardly against the creation of ten additional floor regular situations, and neither the baseline number nor the consequence of an increase is stated. Whether the condition is a precondition or a limitation on staffing is unresolved.

The five additional dayside chauffeurs are not said to be regular situations, unlike the floor positions in the same sentence, and "(4 days and Monday night)" does not state the shift pattern for each. Their status under the chapeau's floor-hire condition is therefore unclear.

The provision requires an update "to reflect the names of the two employees that presently hold these job bids" without naming them or attaching the revised pages 104-5. The content of the amendment is not ascertainable from the writing.

Delivery is to "delivery points designated by the Publisher," an unbounded unilateral discretion with no standard limiting relocation or number of points. "Shall continue to be served" also fixes no baseline practice against which continuation is measured.

This paragraph abolishes the November 22, 1983 West Side Direct Routes Memorandum outright, while the September 9, 1988 Bishow letter ("West Side Directs") says the abolition affects only the attrition portion and leaves every other agreement about those routes intact. The two cannot both be given full effect.

The cross-reference is to "Appendix B-1," but the document contains an "Appendix B" side letter on Honor Boxes and Vending Machines and no Appendix B-1. What is incorporated must be inferred from the instrument as a whole.

"Any existing physical pick-up of such copies shall continue" leaves "such copies" ambiguous between all returns and only the excepted unsold bulldog copies, which are the copies most immediately referred to. The scope of the preserved pick-up practice turns on that antecedent.

The commitment to "maintain present Practices" in honor box and vending machine deliveries defines neither the practices nor the date at which they are frozen, and "The Times direct operation" is broader than the West Side Direct area later described. What must be maintained is left entirely to extrinsic proof.
